fixes.explanation: Not quite, friend. Isaiah doesn't say a few. He says, “The LORD is angry with all the nations and furious with all their armies.” All is a big word. It makes sense that the whole world was called in to listen.
That's it, baker. Isaiah says, “The LORD is angry with all the nations and furious with all their armies.” Not a few, not some. All. And the whole earth gets the call to come near and listen.
You got it, baker. Isaiah says, “Their slain will be left unburied…” I think this is one of the hard lines in the passage. Let's honor that and keep going gently.
Close to a normal ending, but that's not what Isaiah says. He says, “Their slain will be left unburied…” Nothing about a valley or a burial. It's a heavy line, friend.
Yes, baker! Isaiah says, “All the stars of heaven will be dissolved.” Now the message isn't just about the ground under our feet. It reaches all the way up to the stars and the skies.

A covenant is a promise, friend, and that's not the word here. Isaiah says, “For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom.” The lambs, goats and rams show up earlier in that same verse. Sacrifice is the word that belongs.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says, “For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.” So the year of recompense is for Zion's cause. Keep that name in your pocket as we head into the next stop.

Egypt is a big name, friend, but it's not in this verse. Isaiah says, “For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.” The blank is Zion. It's the cause the year of recompense is for.

Assyria doesn't show up in this verse, friend. Isaiah says, “For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.” Zion is the name that fills the blank. The year of recompense is for its cause.
Not this time, friend. Isaiah says the fire will not be quenched, day or night. No morning rescue and no fire going out. Its smoke will ascend forever.
Right, baker. Isaiah says, “From generation to generation it will lie desolate…” Desolate means ruined and abandoned. It stays that way for generation after generation.

Crowded is about as far from it as you can get, friend. Isaiah says, “From generation to generation it will lie desolate…” That means ruined and abandoned. He even adds that no one will ever again pass through it.

Rebuilt would be a nice ending, friend, but that's not what Isaiah says. He says, “From generation to generation it will lie desolate…” Desolate means ruined and abandoned. He even adds that no one will ever again pass through it.
You got it, baker. Isaiah says, “The desert owl and screech owl will possess it, and the great owl and raven will dwell in it.” That's a lot of feathers moving in. Edom gets new residents.
That's it, baker. Isaiah says, “No nobles will be left to proclaim a king…” Without nobles, there's no one from that group to name a king. The line ends with her princes coming to nothing.
Soldiers aren't named here, friend. Isaiah says, “No nobles will be left to proclaim a king…” Nobles are the ones missing. The verse ends with her princes coming to nothing.

You got it, baker. Isaiah says, “Her towers will be overgrown with thorns, her fortresses with thistles and briers.” Towers and fortresses end up covered in prickly weeds. That's a long way from a king's front door.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, “Not one of these will go missing, not one will lack her mate…” Not one is lost. Every creature is accounted for.

Feeding them is a kind thought, friend, but it's not what Isaiah says. He says it's “…because He has ordered it by His mouth, and He will gather them by His Spirit.” The reason is the LORD's order. Isaiah also says no one will ever again pass through Edom.
